speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON PUBLIC HOUSING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have indicated to hon. members on a number of occasions that I would be making a statement on the public housing program after some extension of our own reviews and after I received the opinions of each of the provinces. I am pleased to say that, having completed that review of these submissions, I am now in a position to describe some steps which I propose to take which, I am confident, will improve public housing in quantity and quality.
Hon. members will recall, perhaps, that when I presented the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation budget on February 2 I indicated that our commitments for the low-income housing program, including public housing, in 1969 were for some 27,500 units and that this figure was expected to rise to some 35,000 units in 1970. Taken together, commitments for these two years would amount to approximately 75 per cent of all production undertaken in this field in the last 20 years.
As hon. members are aware, a substantial portion of these starts, to which I have just referred, will come from the $200 million fund temporarily reserved for the building of low-income housing of a kind or in circumstances that are likely to yield information or experience which could lead to innovations in the field. About this program I will have more to say within the next few days.
My own studies in all parts of Canada have given me a deep concern, which I know is shared by many hon. members, not only about numbers of units built or projected but about the form, quality, location and management of public housing, and about equity in the matter of rents. It is with these considerations in mind that we have decided on a number of steps which will have a

significant effect, not only on the quality of new low-income housing but on the more effective utilization and management of existing units.
I would like to deal first, since it is a matter of immediate concern to a great number of people, with the matter of rents for public housing. We have proposed to the provinces a revised rent-to-income scale which we feel reflects more closely the realities of the cost of living and the housing market. These proposed revisions are intended to correct deficiencies in the present rent structure. They have, of course, to do with income as it is used in calculating rents; they have to do with security from sudden rent increases; and they have to do with family needs. Just to put these proposals into some kind of prospective, I would like to review briefly the existing situation.
At the present time tenants in public housing who are receiving welfare payments pay an amount of rent that is equal to the shelter payments which they receive from the welfare agency. AH other tenants pay a rent based on their income. The present rent range is from 16.7 per cent of the low to 30 per cent of the higher level of income. I might say that this 30 per cent rate was set at a time when families who had reached this level of income could perhaps have reasonably been expected to find accommodation for themselves on the open market. It was expected that at this stage of income they would move into other accommodation.
In the present market, however, many families, particularly those with a large number of children, have a great deal of difficulty in finding other accommodation when they reach the income level at which the 30 per cent rate comes into effect. They are, by necessity, obliged to stay on in public housing even though they are paying what amounts to an exorbitant and uneconomic rent. In two provinces, Ontario and Newfoundland, this situation has resulted in provincial action to freeze the rents of such tenants.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Since the level of assistance is based on the simple criterion of income, it imposes a substantially greater burden on a family with five or six children than on a family with one

April 21, 1970
Housing
or two children. Although their incomes are the same, the large family is less able to pay.
Another inequity arises when a wife goes out to work. Her earnings over $250 a year are regarded as family income and the excess is added to the husband's in arriving at a rent. On the other hand, no compensation is allowed for one-parent families who do not have this opportunity for additional earning power by virtue of being engaged in the whole process of a parent looking after children. For all tenants, under the present scheme additional earnings normally result in additional rent charges almost immediately.
These are some of the inequities which the government would like to deal with in proposing revisions in the matter of rents. For public housing we are proposing that:
1.	Family size should be taken into account in arriving at rents. Taking a family with two children as the base, we are proposing to make a reduction in the rent for each child over that number-for instance, a reduction of $2 per month for each child after the second.
2.	Working wives should be allowed to make substantially more than $250 a year before it is considered as income for the purpose of calculating rent. We are proposing a level of $900 a year.
3.	Similarly, incomes of one-parent families, for the purpose of calculating rents, would be reduced by up to $900.
4.	The portion of income required as rents from families in the higher income ranges would be reduced from 30 per cent to 25 per cent, to avoid imposing undue hardships on tenants, particularly large families, who cannot find alternative accommodation in the present market.
5.	The final revision which we are proposing in the matter of rents is the method of adjusting rents as income changes. At the present time, public housing tenants must notify the housing authority as soon as their income increases and the rent is then raised. We feel all tenants should be entitled to enjoy the security of a fixed rent over a reasonable period of time. For this reason we are prepared to have tenants report their incomes at intervals of two years, at which time any increase in rent would be put into effect as a result of any increase in income. On the other hand, a reduction from the income at which the two-year lease rent was negotiated can be reported at any time and the rent reduced an appropriate amount.
[Mr. Andras.j
Before I leave the subject of rents, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize that any revisions will be undertaken after consultation with the provincial governments and with their co-operation. We recognize the need to build the widest possible latitude into these arrangements so that they will be flexible enough to meet particular local conditions. Some provinces may for various reasons wish to charge rents that are not precisely in accord with the federal scale. In this event it is proposed that the federal subsidy would be either half of the project losses, or half what the losses would have been if the federal scale had been adopted, whichever is less.
We have already held a round of talks with provincial authorities and the initial response indicates a substantial measure of agreement with the objectives we are endeavouring to achieve.
I now wish to deal with some other steps which we are taking which will have a particular effect on new and existing low-income housing.
1.	Social and recreation facilities, in both new and existing public housing projects, will be eligible for federal assistance. The precise nature of these facilities will be negotiated with the agencies concerned. By way of illustration, I am talking about such things as community meeting halls, day care nurseries, paramedical physical facilities in homes for the elderly, and the like.
2.	Duly constituted public housing tenant associations will be assisted with grants. As these groups develop, it is apparent that for the most part they are reasonable, articulate and informed. We feel that this kind of selfhelp activity deserves to be encouraged.
3.	A more progressive attitude to public housing tenants' rights will be encouraged with the publication of a revised and, I hope, more sensitive manual for housing authorities, which will include a model lease.
4.	In co-operation with the provinces we shall undertake formal training programs in public housing management. We are already providing continuing assistance through our research program under part V of the National Housing Act for the further study of public housing performance standards and user requirements.
While it is our firm resolve to increase the quantity of housing for low-income people as expeditiously as possible, no opportunity will be overlooked for improving the physical qualities of new developments to overcome objections to some past projects. Indeed, many

of the design proposals for developments undertaken in 1969 were altered to incorporate recommendations of the task force and suggestions presented to me during my own investigation of projects in all parts of the country. Certainly, for example, there has been strong criticism of the practice of providing public housing primarily in the form of high-rise apartment buildings.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Quite frankly, I was not aware of the implications the hon. member has raised. As far as I am concerned I thought there had been contact made with the opposition party housing critics. Certainly I have been requested a number of times during the last several weeks to make this statement, but I apologize if there is an inconvenience to the House. I hope Your Honour will permit me to continue to tell the House about what I have understood to be a very necessary change that is to be made.
We are very conscious of the need for dispersal of public housing units throughout the community for the reasons that I have given.
The provincial governments generally are in agreement, although they have asked that we avoid precise limitations, by regulation, of the number of units to be clustered by community size. I think I am inclined to agree that it is really not practical to be an absolutist in matters like this.
Another factor that has been given consideration is the whole question of tenant organization and involvement in the management of public housing. We are quite prepared to encourage this sort of thing as a matter of social justice, and we think in turn it will encourage a much healthier outlook and climate all round and remove a major cause of some of the difficulties. Along that line, CMHC has funded a series of seminars on tenant participation through the Canadian Welfare Council which will identify the principles and problems involved.
In conclusion, I should like to assure hon. members that we are moving with all possible speed to meet the urgent requirements of Canadian families who lack the means to acquire proper accommodation. I appreciate the suggestions made by hon. members in all corners of the House in regard to this serious problem. At the same time I should like to say that we are now getting some housing on the ground and are proceeding with a continuous process of innovation and evaluation.
Indeed, in the broader sense the greatest weakness of the public housing program is

Mr. Speaker, I believe that in all fairness I should give some credit to the minister for providing me with this statement at least one hour prior to the time I was to reply to it. I hope his colleagues on the treasury benches will realize that if the minister can do this with a statement of this length they should be able follow suit and do the same thing, rather than make statements to the media outside the House.
For me to comment in great depth or offer severe criticism of the statement of the minister would certainly be like being against motherhood. Keeping that in mind, I believe that some changes have been made which have been long awaited by many people who are concerned about the problem of public housing.
I recall that the housing task force had quite a bit to say about this matter. It indicated that the federal government should initiate a thorough research program into the economic, social and psychological issues of public housing, and went on to recommend that until such a study is completed and assessed, no new large projects should be undertaken.
The psychological area of public housing has given many people concern as to the need for, and perhaps the value of, public housing.
I hope the minister is making some in-depth study of this question. I believe that what is needed in public housing is reform. There is no doubt that what the minister has done is some indication that this is happening.
The new rent scale will, of course, affect many people. In particular, the ability of a tenant to remain on a fixed rental for approximately two years will give him some hope that he will be able to move away from public housing and acquire his own home, though with rising interest rates and the lack of mortgage money I do not know how this is going to be possible.
I am particularly pleased to note that there has been some recognition of the value of tenants' associations. I believe this will bring them closer to where the action is. With 
groups such as this which want some participation in their ultimate destiny increasing in number throughout the country, it is important that the government recognize the effect they can have now and I believe will have in the future. I am also pleased to note that the government has indicated some awareness of the social and recreational needs. This is important in relation to public housing.
Finally, this action is something that we have all awaited. I hope the new policy will give many people who are faced with the very severe problem of housing an opportunity at least to be in a position to acquire housing at reasonable rental scales and perhaps lead in the future to the opportunity to own a home.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to preface my remarks by sincerely thanking the minister in charge of housing for his courtesy and co-operation in sending his statement to the housing critics of the different parties. The statement outlines a rearrangement of and addition to public housing guidelines which will result in some improvement, but it also portrays a fundamental misunderstanding of the problem by the minister, namely, the urgent need for a massive increase in public housing starts. The guidelines do not do anything for the 100,000 families across Canada who are on the long waiting lists for public housing. In Toronto alone there are 18,000 families, representing about 60,000 people, waiting for public housing.
The first and greatest need is more public housing. At the present time public housing represents less than 2 per cent of total housing starts in Canada, whereas in England and in European countries public housing represents between 30 per cent and 40 per cent. Even in our neighbour to the south it represents 5 per cent. Surely our immediate target for public housing should be between 15 per cent and 20 per cent of all housing in Canada.
Public housing has been considered a welfare concept. It should not be considered so. Housing should be a basic human right of all Canadians. They are entitled to clean, warm shelter at a reasonable cost. The minister cannot and should not say, as he did in his statement, that public housing is a regrettable necessity. He has missed the point of what housing should be.
My second major criticism is that the statement does not reflect the need for a
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
proper mix of public housing with private, co-operative and senior citizen housing regardless of income levels. This integrating principle is absolutely necessary if we are to rid ourselves of the social stigma concept of public housing. We cannot continue to build segregation of the poor accommodation and increase the social problems caused by ghetto-like housing developments.
My third criticism concerns the failure to include the right of tenants to purchase public housing units. This would have given a pride of ownership and a stake in the community.
If I may comment briefly on the guidelines set forth, the rent scale revisions are welcome. There is a need for constant review so that the situation outlined by the minister will not occur again. The reduction of the percentage of income for rent from 30 per cent to 25 per cent is a progressive step. The increase in additional income allowable to working wives from $250 to $900 is a little short of $20 a week. The experts claim that the amount should be more like $1,500 which would represent $30 a week income for a working wife.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The two-year lease will give security of tenure and security of fixed rents. The social amenities are a decided improvement. Social and recreational facilities must include day care and counselling centres. The participation of tenants' organizations in management is social justice in action, and I add as a caveat that this participation by tenants must be meaningful rather than mere tokenism.
The minister in charge of housing has been a student of studies. He has always replied in the House when questioned about problems that he and his officials are studying these matters and that they are under consideration. I would hope the minister and his officials would graduate to men of action and that the minister's next statement would include a massive increase in public housing, a proper mix of public housing and other types of housing, and the right of tenants to purchase these public housing units.

On Monday of last week, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) admitted under questioning that the government intended to bring in new legislation concerning the Auditor General. I had reminded the Prime Minister that the Auditor General had been pressing the government to introduce legislation to strengthen his office and to define his duties in a more satisfactory way. I asked the Prime Minister why, instead of proceeding with this legislation, he and his

ministers preferred to pick at the Auditor General and undermine his prestige and authority. The Prime Minister answered, and I quote:
It is not a question of either/or, Mr. Speaker. We believe we shall be able to do both.
There is the Freudian slip. I asked why he did not proceed with the legislation rather than pick on the Auditor General and undermine his authority, and the Prime Minister answered he thought they would be able to do both. Judging from the Prime Minister's answer he intends to make it easier to harass, or escape from, the Auditor General; he intends to give his present attack on the Auditor General the force of law. This would represent a typical manoeuvre on the part of the present government. The Auditor General has been asking for a long time for a review of the legislation governing his office. He has drafted his own proposals for consideration. There is a grave danger that the government will use this request as cover for legislation which will strip him of the power necessary for his office. Then, I suppose, Information Canada will be set in motion to explain that this is what the Auditor General had wanted.
This is not the occasion on which to discuss the contents of legislation. But let the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board understand that if they try a trick like that, not even Information Canada will be able to help them. What members opposite are saying, in effect, is that since the government cannot stand the heat, Mr. Henderson should get out of the kitchen. I presume they want to lock him up in the cellar where no one can see him or hear him.
There are proper and above-board ways in which the government could deal with an Auditor General if it believes he is wrong. If it believes he is incompetent, it has the right to introduce in both Houses a motion for his dismissal. If it believes he is wrong in his criticisms of the government, it has a right, of course, to answer those criticisms in detail before the Public Accounts Committee. The government would rather waste $40 million than have somebody point out the waste so that they could stop it. They have the mentality of a man who, when accused of a crime, tries to fire the policeman.
Consider some of the double-talk which has already come from the government side. The President of the Treasury Board defended his attack on the Auditor General in terms of a switch in government emphasis to "effectiveness rather than efficiency". I find that hard to understand. It sounds very much like something from Alice in Wonderland. This questioning of the work of the Auditor General is based, according to the President of the Treasury Board, upon the emphasis the government is placing on effectiveness rather than upon efficiency. Perhaps somebody else could explain that. This statement by the minister is taken, as a direct quotation, from the "Encounter" transcript. Whatever it means, I do not think Parliament can ignore such a statement. It would be bad enough for a government to renounce a claim to efficiency; it is the only claim the government had. Now, it is gone, like the just society.

After all, efficiency implies you are doing a job. It is the difference between image and action. Another example of double talk is the distinction being made between matters of policy and what I suppose must be called matters of non-policy. As I understand it, that is the distinction that the Prime Minister and the President of the Privy Council would make, and I suppose there is no one better qualified on questions of non-policy. What

Criticism of Auditor General does this distinction mean? The Prime Minister suggested the other day he thought it was wrong that the Auditor General should criticize the payment made by order in council of some $180 million to automobile companies. He said it was wrong to have this kind of criticism from the Auditor General, presumably on the ground that this was a deliberate decision to let the $180 million go.
In other words, when waste is deliberate, the watchdog should be quiet. When waste is deliberate the Auditor General has no right to comment on it, because it then becomes a matter of waste by government policy. That is quite a principle! It will not be long now before the government will argue that the decision to refit the Bonaventure at high cost was a deliberate decision, and therefore should not be investigated. I suppose that if horses were put on the payroll as a matter of deliberate policy, this too would be beyond the comment of the Auditor General.
The government knows that if it is going to close the door on the Auditor General with regard to questions involving policy decisions, it is virtually closing the door completely. After all, this distinction between policy and non-policy from this point of view is not really a distinction at all; it is a dodge that is designed to strip the Auditor General of power without appearing to have removed his power.
As Professor Norman Ward pointed out in his special correspondence in the Ottawa Journal last night, other governments have tried a dodge like that before. This government is original in very few respects. Professor Ward is the author of the standard text on government spending in Canada, called "The Public Purse", and he makes it clear that there is ample precedent for an Auditor General to be concerned with auditing questions involving policy decisions. That has been the practice of the Auditor General whenever and wherever that office has been effective.
This concept goes to the very heart of the power of the Auditor General. Without that power he is just another accountant. With the power to report to the public, through this House, the cost of decisions by the goverment on policy matters, he is a public servant that the government cannot ignore and one of the very best friends that the taxpayer has in Ottawa.
Criticism is, of course, a function of the opposition and one which is more necessary today than ever before. But I do not hesitate

Even with the staff the Auditor General has today we can see what he is reporting, and we can suspect without being too suspicious that we are only seeing, and that he is only finding, the tip of the iceberg.
I suppose someone will say something about all the help the government is giving the opposition in the matter of research staff. I hope that nobody is going to suggest that this is an effective substitute for an efficient and fully powered Auditor General. In any event, I hope nobody on that side of the House will keep repeating this sort of thing in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is spending more money during the course of a few months on answering letters that he has received in connection with the white paper than is available to all opposition parties for research in a full year.
Under this government there is a tendency to secrecy, the use of task forces and confidential studies by consultants which, generally speaking, are not made public. Usually, we do not get the background papers that lie behind government decisions. I say that this policy of secrecy and confidentiality certainly must not be extended. For example, the government has never made public the estimates upon which its decision to abandon the Prince Edward Island causeway was based. That was a high-handed and arrogant attitude shown toward a little province. Perhaps the government will get away with it, I do not know; but we are at any rate grateful that at least the Auditor General can tell the people the cost that has already been incurred as a result of the decision the government made, though the government does not seem to be very happy at having these figures disclosed.
Attacks by ministers on the Auditor General should be seen as part of a larger strategy, a strategy that is designed to control information. It might be thought strange that a government that has proposed and has established Information Canada should at the same point in time attack and try to restrict the operations of the Auditor General. This simply sheds light upon the role of Information Canada as seen by the ministers of this government, and sheds further light upon the government's refusal to agree to the establishment of some kind of ombudsman to watch over Information Canada. Indeed, what makes this attack on the Auditor General so alarming is that it does not stand alone: it is part 
of a pattern of deliberate actions by this government to build up its own power and to break down the power of its critics.
The attack on Parliament came first. Here, the government showed so much contempt for this institution that it used closure to impose a rule that was so badly drafted it would not work. That attitude is clear in the establishment of a propaganda agency. It follows an ill-conceived move by the President of the Privy Council to bring about a change in the chairmanship of the public accounts committee, presumably because that chairman was being too independent.
Following this the Auditor General came under attack. The government is not only adding to its own power; it has set a deliberate course to silence or at least to weaken the critics whose powers had previously been established precisely to check the abuse of the power of government. The Canadian public and the members of this House require hard information, particularly about financial matters rather than the kind of pap that may be provided by Information Canada. What is required is the hard kind of information that is provided by the Auditor General of this country, whether the government likes it or not.

Sir, it is my experience that criticism from an officer like the Auditor General ought to be helpful to a government. When I became the premier of Nova Scotia there was no Auditor General. There was a sort of a balance sheet audit, and apparently the government is seeking to return to it. We established an Auditor General. From time to
April 21. 1970	COMMONS
time, certain reports of the Auditor General
are annoying, but there is no question about it, they make for better government. An Auditor General can point up mistakes when they are small enough to stop. He will often be far more searching in his examination and more frank in his comment than members of a cabinet would be. By virtue of his access to the public service he can often find mistakes more quickly than a parliamentary opposition can. He can help the government spot mistakes and stop mistakes before they get too far out of control.
Certainly, this attack on the Auditor General is not designed to improve the efficiency of government operations. Sometimes, of course, the criticisms of an Auditor General will combine with public opinion to force a government to change its course. This, of course, is one of the risks of a democracy. The point of government is not always to get its own way and to bulldoze its programs through. The point is to implement a program which meets public needs and will stand public criticism. In any event, the importance of an effective Auditor General increases and will continue to increase as the role of government increases. The role of government is increasing rapidly and it seems likely it will continue to grow both in size and complexity. The cost of government is going up, as is the amount of money it has to spend or to waste. That will be particularly so if the government succeeds in smuggling through massive tax increases under the guise of tax reform.
I suggest what should be done with the Auditor General is to increase his power, not reduce it. I would think this would be the obvious course to be supported by any true friend of democracy in Canada. With a government increasing in size and complexity, the Auditor General's powers ought to be increased. Certainly, it is wrong to harass and undermine this important official. It is important to this House at this time to assert its support for this watchdog, and assert the support of this House for the role of the Auditor General against an arrogant and over-riding government. Therefore, I do ask the House and call upon its members to support the motion I have the honour to present to it this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, the main motion to which we are addressing ourselves is very ingeniously constructed. The only problem is that it is based on a false premise. Let me read the second half of it:
That this House ... reasserts its support of the principle of unfettered parliamentary scrutiny of government expenditures including the right of the Auditor General to comment on the failure of the government to make expenditure in strict compliance with parliamentary appropriations and to report on these and any other cases he feels should be brought to the attention of Parliament.
This statement puts forward principles which are unexceptionable. Everyone in this House can agree with this affirmation. Indeed, it comes close to paraphrasing the provisions of the Financial Administration Act, a law of this Parliament. The first part of the motion alleges that the government has criticized the Auditor General of Canada "for carrying out his duties according to law". This simply is not the case.
The whole of the motion, as I have said, is based on a false premise. It is utterly fundamental that in the parliamentary system there be an officer of Parliament above politics, above policy differences and above partisan debates who ensures for Parliament and the public that the government and its civil servants are acting with legality and probity in the discharge of their duties. I hold this view. The government holds this view. It is for this very reason that I, and some of my colleagues, have admitted to some concern when the Auditor General has been cast in the role of policy critic, in the role of adversary in contests over public policy.
The Auditor General has submitted to the Public Accounts Committee a draft bill with respect to his office. The government had intended to express there its views as to the duties of the Auditor General, the independence which befits his office and other issues which the Auditor General himself has raised. We are now in the position of being obliged, unfortunately, in the context of a highly partisan debate to make known our general approach to the bill which has been submitted.
There are four general issues which emerge from recent reports of the Auditor General: the independence of the Auditor General
April 21. 1970

Criticism of Auditor General from the government and from the Acts of Parliament which govern the public service; the role and responsibilities of the Auditor General; the responsibility of the government to respond to the criticisms he advances in his reports and the status of the Auditor General and his office. I will speak to each of these in turn.
The Auditor General has made certain proposals which would assure his independence from the normal rules which govern the civil service, thus by inference further affirming his independence of the government. The government has been prepared to accept the Auditor General's propositions, and indeed to go even further than he has proposed.
The Auditor General has suggested that he be freed of any limitation by government on the number of employees he engages, and of any restraints on the salaries which he may pay them. By implication he would be free, too, himself to bargain with the employees' union. To these proposals, the government takes no exception.
We have been inclined to look to the Public Accounts Committee for its view on the Auditor General's proposals. We see three or four questions to which the committee might usefully address itself. First, we assume that the committee and the Auditor General alike would want to find a mechanism which would avoid the situation in which any office has unlimited access to public funds. Secondly, the committee might suggest some method, other than the Treasury Board, for determining the classification and pay of the staff in the Auditor General's office. And thirdly, we would draw to the attention of the committee, with respect to personnel appointments, that this House has already designated the Public Service Commission as the protector of the merit system: we would observe that to transfer the power of appointment from this body to the Auditor General would be to transfer responsibility from one office reporting to Parliament to another. The committee might wish to hear from both the Public Service Commission and the Auditor General on this question.
One approach which might be used to free the Auditor General from the restraints which apply on the civil service would be to provide that he should report to the House of Commons through the Speaker, as does the Commissioner of Official Languages. This would give the Auditor General even greater freedom from the rules which apply to the civil service than he has proposed, and would

substitute only those provisions which this House itself applies in respect of the Speaker's staff.
The government has been considering this
alternative, as well as the one put forward by the Auditor General himself, and would commend them to the Public Accounts Committee for consideration.
I will now deal with the duties of the Auditor General. The second issue which has arisen from the Auditor General's report is the duties which Parliament has assigned to him. I should like to make it abundantly clear, Mr. Speaker, that the government has at no time taken exception to the legislative outline of these duties. For our part, we support the wording of section 67 of the Financial Administration Act and the duties which flow from it in succeeding sections. Let me quote section 67:
The Auditor General shall examine in such manner as he may deem necessary the accounts relating to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and to public property and shall ascertain whether in his opinion
(a)	the accounts have been faithfully and properly kept,
(b)	all public money has been fully accounted for, and the rules and procedures applied are sufficient to secure an effective check on the assessment, collection and proper allocation of the revenue,

(d)	essential records are maintained and the rules and procedures applied are sufficient to safeguard and control public property.
What does this mean, in non-legal terms? It means that the government believes the Auditor General has the right and the responsibility to comment both on the soundness of the financial controls being exercised by the government, and on the probity and legality with which ministers and civil servants are discharging their duties. Let me repeat; the Auditor General has a duty to comment on the probity of the government of this land-by which I mean simply that he has a duty to protect the taxpayers' dollars. And his right and his ability to do this must be protected.
These words cast a very wide net: I know it, and approve it. After all, hon. members should remember that the President of the Treasury Board and the Auditor General have common concerns. The government looks to the Treasury Board to establish the
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
internal procedures and audits which will ensure probity and legality in the civil service, just as this House looks to the Auditor General to ensure that we have indeed succeeded in achieving this goal. The success of the Treasury Board depends in no small measure, then, upon the existence of the Auditor General and his legislative postaudit. It depends, too, upon the independence and impartiality of his office.
It is for this very reason that I have, when questioned about the Auditor General's role, expressed concern that it not be looked upon as an adversary role; that his office not be envisioned as a source of criticism of government policy or of statutes of Parliament. Probity and legality, yes; government policy and parliamentary decisions, no.
The reasons for this position are not hard to find, Mr. Speaker. Policy questions clearly are matters of judgment, matters about which political parties differ and ought to be expected to differ. They engage us in debate in this House; they engage us in political or party differences which ultimately must be resolved by the electorate. Questions of probity on the other hand are above politics: no one disputes that the highest ethical standards ought and must obtain in the government of this country.
Herein lies the distinction which I have observed should apply. If the Auditor General comments on, or is expected to comment on, policy questions, sooner or later he will, by inference, become engaged in partisan differences. He will appear sooner or later to be taking sides in matters which are the subject of political debate. If the Auditor General is cast in this role by the duties Parliament imposes upon him, his independence and his effectiveness will have been endangered.
We should remember, I think, that the Public Service of Canada enjoys, not only in Canada but elsewhere in the world, an enviable and deserved reputation for probity-and absence of corruption and dishonesty. This is a priceless asset. It is a reputation which depends in no small measure on the certificate of the Auditor General, a certificate which proclaims the probity and legality with which government-any government-is performing its duties. The credibility of this certificate, whatever it says, must not be called into question. But if the Auditor General is cast in an adversary role, if he appears by reason of the duties we impose upon him to be an officer of the opposition-which I think 22218-41

Let me hasten to add, Mr. Speaker, that criticism of policy there must be. That goes without saying. But it must come from elected representatives. It is up to the opposition to interrogate, to query, to debate, to criticize the policies of the government. But they should not seek to enlist the Auditor General as their ally. If they do they will destroy his office. A staff to assist the opposition, yes; the government recently acted to enlarge this staff. The government believes that there is room for improvement here. We will be proposing that the government ought to be obliged to report to Parliament, to the Public Accounts Committee, on the totality of the Auditor General's report, on all the criticisms he has made of the government and the public service. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is my duty to speak to this nonconfidence motion. I have been a member of the public accounts committee for about the same length of time as the present Auditor General has acted in this capacity. I have always had a great admiration for the efficient and businesslike manner in which he has presented his reports. We are all aware of the fact that government business involves spending more money than any other business in Canada spends. This gives us an indication of the vast responsibilities that are undertaken by the Auditor General and his staff.
At the outset, I should like to put on the record the statute that sets up the office of Auditor General so that the people across this nation may fully understand the position of the Auditor General. I know this point has been commented upon by several speakers before me, but only in part, and I think that the full picture should be given to the House.
Criticism of Auditor General Therefore, I should like to quote section 65 of the Financial Administration Act, 1967, which provides as follows:
(1)	The Governor in Council shall by commission under the Great Seal of Canada appoint an officer called the Auditor General of Canada to hold office during good behaviour until he attains the age of sixty-five years, but he is removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
(2)	The Auditor General shall out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund be paid a salary of thirty thousand dollars per annum.
(3)	The provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act, except those relating to tenure of office, apply to the Auditor General.
(4)	Such officers and employees as are necessary to enable the Auditor General to perform his duties shall be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act.
(5)	The Governor in Council may appoint a person temporarily to perform the duties of the Auditor General during a vacancy in the office of Auditor General.
Section 66 provides:
(1)	Notwithstanding any act, the Auditor General is entitled to free access at all convenient times to all files, documents and other records relating to the accounts of every department, and he is also entitled to require and receive from members of the public service such information, reports and explanations as he may deem necessary for the proper performance of his duties.
(2)	The Auditor General may station in any department any person employed in his office to enable him more effectively to carry out his duties, and the department shall provide the necessary office accommodation for any such officer so stationed.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
(3)	The Auditor General shall require every person employed in his office who is to examine the accounts of a department pursuant to this Act to comply with any security requirements applicable to, and to take any oath of secrecy required to be taken by persons employed in that department.
(4)	The Auditor General may suspend from the performance of his duty any person employed in his office.
67.	The Auditor General shall examine in such manner as he may deem necessary the accounts relating to the Consolidated Revenue Fund and to public property and shall ascertain whether in his opinion
(a)	the accounts have been faithfully and properly kept,
(b)	all public money has been fully accounted for, and the rules and procedures applied are sufficient to secure an effective check on the assessment, collection and proper allocation of the revenue,
(c)	money has been expended for the purposes for which it was approved by Parliament, and the expenditures have been made as authorized, and
(d)	essential records are maintained and the rules and procedures applied are sufficient to safeguard and control public property.

i (a) make such examination of the accounts and records of each registrar as he deems necessary, and such other examinations of a registrar's transactions as the Minister may require, and

and may, by arrangement with the registrar, maintain custody and control, jointly with the registrar, maintain custody and control, jointly with the registrar, of cancelled and unissued securities.

70.	(1) The Auditor General shall report annually to the House of Commons the results of his examinations and shall call attention to every case in which he has observed that
(a)	any officer or employee has wilfully or negligently omitted to collect or receive any money belonging to Canada,
(b)	any public money was not duly accounted for and paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund,
(c)	any appropriation was exceeded or was applied to a purpose or in a manner not authorized by Parliament,
(d)	an expenditure was not authorized or was not properly vouched or certified
(e)	there has been a deficiency or loss through the fraud, default or mistake of any- person, or
(f)	a special warrant authorized the payment of any money, and to any other case that the Auditor General considers should be brought to the notice of the House of Commons.
(2) The report of the Auditor General shall be laid before the House of Commons by the Minister on or before the 31st day of December, or, if' Parliament is not then in session, within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session and if the Minister does not, within the time prescribed by this section, present the report to the House of Commons, the Auditor General shall transmit the report to the Speaker for tabling in the House of Commons.
71.	The Auditor General shall, whenever the Governor in Council, the Treasury Board or the Minister directs, inquire into and report on any matter relating to the financial affairs of Canada or to public property and on any person or organization that has received financial aid from the Government of Canada or in respect of which financial aid from the Government of Canada is sought.
72.	Any report of the Auditor General to the Governor in Council or the Treasury Board shall be made through the Minister.
73.	Whenever it appears to the Auditor General that any public money has been improperly retained by any person, he shall forthwith report the circumstances of such cases to the Minister.
74.	The Auditor General may examine any person on oath on any matter pertaining to any account subject to audit by him and for the purposes of|

any such examination the Auditor General may exercise all the powers of a commissioner under Part I of the Inquiries Act.
75.	An officer of the public service nominated by the Treasury Board shall examine and certify to the House of Commons in accordance with the outcome of his examinations the receipts and disbursements of the office of the Auditor General.
Government ministers who make accusations against the Auditor General are familiar with the act, but rather than act like men and make charges in the House of Commons they have used methods that are not acceptable to this House and not in keeping with the high offices they are privileged to hold. Public opinion indicates there is much resentment of this unjustifiable criticism of a good, honest public servant.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, this is not the first attempt to demoralize the public accounts committee and its administrators. It was only a few weeks ago that a subtle and despicable move was made to remove the chairman of the committee. That particular government strategy failed miserably because the committee unanimously gave the chairman a vote of confidence on their first opportunity following the intended leak to the press by the conspirators. The government has been embarrassed by their own careless and frivolous handling of the public purse, and to try and save face they resort to pulling a red herring across the trail. What they have done could only be termed childish and immature.
The Auditor General has a reputation above reproach. He is highly respected in his profession, not only in Canada but by the fraternity of the United Nations which embraces over 100 countries. He has had the enviable distinction of being chosen by them to be their external auditor. In view of the confidence the United Nations has placed in him, does it not seem a little ridiculous for this government to whimper about something of very little significance? This government has not paid enough attention to the information that has been revealed by the Auditor General and which, if heeded, could have saved the country millions of dollars. Rather, they go on their merry way spending like drunken sailors and at the same time telling all segments of our economy that they must tighten their belts.
I need only mention a few of their recent extravagant orgies to demonstrate their insincerity in respect of fightiing inflation. It was recently made known to this House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) needs over $820,000 to maintain his office and staff, as
April 21. 1970	COMMONS
compared to $50,000 to do the same job when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister. Only two years ago, the Prime Minister of that day operated his office on $75,000.
Then, we have the new agency, Information Canada, which, from all indications, will be infringing on the responsibilities of Members of Parliament, confusing and frustrating them and costing the country millions of dollars. Another expenditure we could well get along without is the $50 million or more that will be spent by the Bilingual and Biculturalism Commission which can only be termed a superfluous expenditure. I presume the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee will not have the opportunity of scrutinizing many such items.
The people of the country were astounded when, through the Auditor General and the Public Accounts Committee, the facts in respect of the refit of the Bonaventure were made known. The colossal blundering by government representatives in their estimating, in their supervision and their judgment, was almost unbelievable. The people of Canada were led down the garden path to the extent of many millions of dollars by the extraordinary handling of government responsibilities.
I could go on and enumerate many more transactions brought to the attention of the Public Accounts Committee by the Auditor General, but since the details of the Bonaventure case are so well known, I think it illustrates the valuable and efficient work the Auditor General has been doing over the years.
The Public Accounts Committee has been aware for quite some time of the fact that the Auditor General has only been doing a spot check on expenditures. He has brought to the attention of the committee that his staff is insufficient to do a thorough job. The Public Accounts Committee, in its reports to the government, has made several appeals to have the Auditor General given the authority to take on the necessary staff to do a complete and thorough audit of all government transactions. To my knowledge, the government has turned a deaf ear to this request-in fact, his staff has been reduced. This made it obvious that they would take the first opportunity to clip the Auditor General's wings.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) recently availed himself of a good chance when he appeared on television. His first remark was that the Auditor General should stick to assessing the government's accounting procedure. In replying to that

As to the Minister's second statement, he had his foot in his mouth when he wondered whether the Auditor General should cast himself in this role or whether we should look for really another kind of person to be Auditor General. The Prime Minister, (Mr. Trudeau) when questioned in the House by the Leader of the Opposition as to whether or not this statement was government policy, made a flimsy reply in an attempt to cover up for the arrogance of the President of the Treasury Board when he said, as recorded at page 5771 of Hansard:

I have no hesitation in saying that the people across the country, if given the opportunity, would endorse the work of the Auditor General and give him an overwhelming vote of confidence.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of the motion that has been moved today by the Leader of the Opposition. I speak with some concern for the motion presently before the House. I do so with a sense of responsibility as a member of the House of Commons for some 13 years, a considerable number of these years spent as a member of the Public Accounts Committee. Once a year a slim, innocuous looking grey book makes its appearance in Ottawa, a book which has jokingly been referred to as "Henderson's financial follies". This book does not contain a script for a follies show at the National Arts Centre, although some of the short stories it confains would make a suitable script for light comedy if some of the facts were not so tragic to our Canadian taxpayers.
When the Auditor General's report is tabled in the Commons all hell breaks loose for within its covers are set forth the sins, errors and omissions of government departments, public agencies and Crown corporations for the past 12 months. Careers have been made and broken through information in this book s pages. Policies have been examined, changed or even abandoned under the battering of an accounting which every year sees opposition members gleefully searching for rocks to throw at the treasury benches while government supporters scramble for cover. Behind this parliamentary tornado is a neat, grey, cleanshaven public servant named Maxwell Henderson. To a deadly serious job, he brings the saving graces of quick humour and an easy charm more suited to politics
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
than to accounting. His reports are stiff, rigid and righteous, but in talking to him we find that he is friendly and co-operative. He brings to his position a sense of duty and a sense of humour, both of which are needed on Parliament Hill.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
When Mr. Watson Sellars retired in 1960, Mr. Henderson was appointed by the then Minister of Finance, Hon. Donald Fleming. In my opinion and in the opinion of most Canadians he has fulfilled his duties capably and well since that time.

Like a judge, the Auditor General is a servant of Parliament, not a servant of the cabinet. He can be fired only by a joint resolution of the House of Commons and the Senate, a step which has never even been threatened in Canada until the present time. In my opinion the Auditor General is the watchdog of the public purse and he is in need of the independence guaranteed him by the Financial Administration Act under which he operates. I say this because his main function is to see that every cent of public moneys is properly accounted for. This makes him one of the most feared and possibly one of the most disliked public servants in the nation. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, he is not popular with the present government, but to the best of my knowledge he has always carried out his duties without fear or favour.
When the Conservative administration which appointed Mr. Henderson decided to scrap the Avro Arrow in 1959, a replacement had to be found but noisy complaints were heard in the House of Commons about the $400 million write-off on the Arrow and any additional expenditures would only add fuel to the fire. The Department of National Defence hit on the solution of making a swap with the United States. In return for 66 F-10 Voodoo interceptors, Canada undertook to operate a number of Pinetree Line radar stations for the Americans so our defence requirements would be met without the need of a heavy cash outlay.
The whole deal seemed to be smooth and acceptable until the Auditor General caught up with it. In his 1960 report he rebuked the defence chiefs for not showing the Voodoos as an expense. Whether they were paid for in cash or work, he pointed out, they cost money. He went on to estimate the outlay at $170 million and this provided a ripe tomato 22218-42

Criticism of Auditor General for opposition spokesmen, who were Liberal in that day, to toss across the Commons at the government which was Conservative and had just appointed Mr. Henderson.
Within a year he was involved in another head-on clash with the Conservative administration. The Revenue Department had held up wages to three men on the public payroll for non-payment of income tax. Mr. Henderson's investigators became intrigued and asked for the tax files of the three delinquents. The Hon. George Nowlan was then Minister of National Revenue and he refused the request. Mr. Henderson made note of this refusal in his next report to Parliament.
The minister was vigorously grilled at that time by the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, as our leader in the House used to call them in those days. He was grilled in the House of Commons almost immediately, where he let slip that the three men involved were MP's, two Conservatives and one Liberal. The fight was carried before the Public Accounts Committee where the minister stood his ground on a provision of the Income Tax Act, which guarantees secrecy in income tax matters. However, Mr. Henderson pointed to the Financial Administration Act which entitles him to access to "all files, documents, or other reports, notwithstanding any other legislation." The Auditor General won his point and the files were produced.
It is my contention that in both these cases Mr. Henderson's concern was not to embarrass the government-although that happened-but rather it was to ensure the proper accounting of funds to the taxpayer. If the Commons votes to spend $10 million on fish, that is of no concern to the Auditor General, but if the money appropriated for fish is spent on chips, then the Auditor General is very much involved. I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that at no time during these investigations was there any suggestion by the then Progressive Conservative government that the criticisms of the Auditor General were invalid or that any action should be taken against him.
What has caused this issue to be raised today, Mr. Speaker? All of us throughout the length and breadth of this nation were disturbed when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) recently told a television audience that the Auditor General is pitting his judgment against the government and that he should stick to assessing the government's accounting procedures. The minister went on to wonder whether Mr. Henderson
April 21, 1970

Criticism of Auditor General should pit his judgment against the government or whether the government should really look for another kind of person to be Auditor General. Why are we, as Canadians, concerned over statements which have been made on this matter by the President of the Treasury Board and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)? Why are we concerned when our Prime Minister indicates he plans to introduce legislation into this House defining the authority and scope of the activities of the Auditor General?
We are concerned about the erosion and destruction of the power of Parliament. That is why this motion has been raised today.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Some years ago Lord Chesterfield said:
Let us consider that arbitrary power has seldom or never been introduced into any country at once. It must be introduced by slow degrees and as it were, step by step, lest the people should see it approach.
We are now viewing the acquisition of arbitrary power which is the planned and plotted objective of the Trudeau government. This government wants power that is above restraint and beyond criticism. This government wants arbitrary power that is introduced by slow degrees, step by step, sometimes stealthily, sometimes openly with sly hypocrisy, sometimes with snare and sometimes by trap, sometimes with soothing syrup or a slogan. Whatever the moves, they are always directed and ever advancing toward one objective, namely, absolute arbitrary power.
It is the tragedy of political liberty that men, once they have attained it, assume the battle won not only for themselves but also for future generations. The historians paint these long gone battles, fought by men against their oppressive rulers, on a grand and dramatic scale. They hang them in a frame of large events. Here I refer to King John signing the Magna Carta and Cromwell dismissing a corrupt Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, all this happened in the long gone past. We as Canadians do not expect, and believe there is no need for, such a dramatic confrontation today. We sometimes forget these symbolic pictures of the past only represent the ultimate recovery of our political liberties. We do not ask, over what long period, in what undramatic ways, were these liberties first lost or gained. We forget we lost them, fought for them and recovered 
them in Nova Scotia, in Quebec, in Ontario and in the west. We forget that our cousins to the south fought for them, and only won them in a bloody revolution. We are not mindful in our history of the little things, Our editorials, which are the daily history of our times, contain nothing like this leader from the London Times of August, 1846:
The greatest tyranny has the smallest beginnings. From precedents overlooked, from remonstrations despised, from grievances treated with ridicule, from powerless men oppressed with impunity, and overbearing men tolerated with complacence, springs the tyrannical usage which generations of wise and good men may hereafter perceive and lament and resist in vain.
At present, common minds no more see a crushing tyranny in a trivial unfairness, or a ludicrous indignity, than the eye, uninformed by reason, can discern the oak in the acorn, or the utter desolution of winter in the first autumnal fall. Hence the necessity of denouncing with unwearied and even troublesome perseverance, a single act of oppression. Let it alone and it stands on record. The country has allowed it and when it is at last provoked to a late indignation, it finds itself gagged with the record of its own ill compulsion.
This government, Mr. Speaker, has progressed some distance along the way to arbitrary power. The criticism of the Auditor General of Canada is only a prelude to their plans and is but one of the most recent and most dramatic in a series of steps along the path. We have every reason to be concerned when a government is bold enough to attack a publicly paid critic of the government who is himself by reason of his criticisms so much in the public eye.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This type of criticism is inexcusable. This government was elected to office on a platform of two slogans, one being that the government would establish in Canada the just society and the other that Canadians would enjoy participatory democracy. Journalists have attributed the slogan, "The just society'' to Palto's democratic philosophy of government. But, Mr. Speaker, we do not need political philosophies in this country to tell us what to do. In ten words, let us have-government of the people, by the people, for the people.
We have seen the symptoms in this House, Mr. Speaker, which should concern all Canadians: the step-by-step whittling away of our procedural rights; the two efforts to change the rules to impose the guillotine upon debate and criticism; the attempt to change the non-partisan chairman of the Public Accounts Committee; the interference with
April 21, 1970

committees and the presentation of committee reports; the establishment of the ministerial roster system; the establishment of corporations and agencies which remove whole areas of public affairs from the investigation and scrutiny of members; the delegation of vast law-making powers to the cabinet; the appointment of officials at Her Majesty's pleasure and not during good behaviour; the unpublicized introduction of a bill to seize vast economic and financial power by the socialization of private investment, which was aborted in the other place; the bill now before the House to take over control of the entire farm products industry from farmer to consumer; the large increase of officials at the decision advisory level, and bills which provide for public hearings that are not public hearings. I could go on, Mr. Speaker, but time does not permit. These are the steps this government has taken or is taking along the path to arbitrary power. They are known to members of this House and have been fought against by members of all opposition parties. Unfortunately, they are not known generally to the public.

speechtext:
The opposition has chosen this subject for special attention on an allotted day because it has thus been enabled to introduce a motion of want of confidence in the government. The role or function of the Auditor General would not have been brought into special focus except for two circumstances that I presume gave rise to the motion before us. One of those was certain recent comments by two members of the cabinet who have been referred to, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald). Those remarks have been referred to. The other circumstance is the legislation to come before this House, to be known as the Auditor General of Canada Act.
Dealing with each of these sources of complaint separately, I note that the remarks attributed to the President of the Privy Council have been noted several times already today. In the remarks complained of, which were uttered on television a short time ago, it was said that any disagreement with the Auditor General did not stem from his criticizing accounting procedures, the basic practices involved, the method of expenditure, and so on, but rather from his criticisms of underlying government policy. That statement stands on the record. The transcript of the television interview has been referred to and has now been noted as a source of complaint by the opposition.
I note as well that the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board, who has already spoken in this debate, were referred to by the Leader of the Opposition when he led off this afternoon's debate. I am always a little suspicious, Mr. Speaker, when a very short quota-

Criticism of Auditor General tion is lifted from a long transcript and referred to in this kind of debate. Having heard the short quotation referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, I took the liberty of looking at the original transcript of the television program that was referred to.
I note on page 10 of that transcript, almost two pages before the paragraph that has been referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, that the subject was expanded somewhat. It might be interesting to read those remarks, as the Leader of the Opposition should have done out of a sense of fairness, and include the remarks already referred to and attributed to the President of the Treasury Board. The Leader of the Opposition at least might have had the decency to read all of that passage to the House so that we might be fully informed.
This interview was being conducted by Mr. Collister and Mr. Lynch, of great notoriety in this chamber. Mr. Lynch asked this question, as recorded at the bottom of page 10 of the transcript:
If you're so hot on efficiency and the things you've just been talking about, why is the Auditor General, Mr. Maxwell Henderson, so unimpressed with the way public business is conducted, and why is he so critical of the Treasury Board for cutting down on the staff that he has to make sure that efficiency and productivity are maintained? You and he seem to be butting heads against one another.
The	President	of	the	Treasury	Board
answered:
Well to use a phrase you applied a little earlier, one would expect him to have a vested interest in discovering things which are subject to criticism. That's his job.
Mr. Lynch then said:
Right. He says you're throttling him. You're not giving him enough staff and enough money.
The	President	of	the	Treasury	Board
answered:
The fact of the matter, is, as has been pointed out on a number of occasions, he has not, to the best of my knowledge, ever filled out the establishment that he has had authorized. And I mentioned earlier that the civil service has now had, as a whole, cut back from its authorizations for numbers of people far in excess of what they ever had or seemed to be likely to get. The same kind of operation was applied to the Auditor General, and indeed the authorization for very large numbers which he had never reached, was reduced to something quite modestly in excess of his existing staff. So he still has room to increase his staff.
Reporting the full text of that interview, it seems to me, places in an entirely different perspective the remarks of the President of the Treasury Board; and to be fair, if those remarks are the source of the opposition's 
DEBATES	April 2L 1970
criticism, opposition members should have had the decency to read into the record the whole transcript. In other words, the remarks made by both hon. gentlemen simply refer to the fact that it is clearly understood that the function of the Auditor General, a function he has carried out so well, is to criticize the manner in which the government spends funds and say whether that spending is wasteful, spendthrift or even inefficient.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The policy underlying the decision to authorize the expenditure of those dollars is the prerogative of Parliament. It is not an area for the Auditor General to exercise his criticism. Having accepted as policy of this House that certain dollars are to be expended, it is the job of the Auditor General to examine very carefully and criticize fully and completely if those dollars are not properly spent or if the expenditure of the moneys or the accounting for them is not properly done.
Even in my short experience in this House I have found that the report of the Auditor General for 1968-69 is a very complete document, detailing some very large and wasteful expenditures on the part of the government. To suggest that the Auditor General is being restricted in his job of criticizing this government is ludicrous. The reports of the Auditor General are detailed to a degree I would not have imagined possible. I submit they are very clear. It is for this reason I and other members oppose the motion and support the remarks that have been made with respect to the function of the Auditor General. The Auditor General should criticize in the way that he has done in his report. However, it is not his job to criticize policy decisions of this Parliament. That is the prerogative of this Parliament, the news media and others who wish to criticize, but it is not the job of the Auditor General.
The source of complaint is the remarks I have referred to, or the forthcoming legislation setting up a special act of Parliament with regard to the Auditor General. Let us examine the position of the government and its attitude in respect of this legislation. I submit it is significant to note that this bill was not drafted by the government. It was not prepared by a government draftsman who was subject to any control, political pressure or authority of this government. It is extremely significant to note that the proposed Auditor General's act was prepared, at the request of Parliament, by the Auditor General.

It contains authority which is extraordinary in the process of legislation. It was drafted in the initial stages by the Auditor General.
One of the first steps, a very wise one, taken by the committee was to refer the proposed legislation to the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants which made a very detailed analysis of it. It was returned to the Public Accounts Committee with some very thorough and comprehensive recommendations about the legislation-and the manner in which it deals with all the functions of the Auditor General. Surely no one can-suggest from the behaviour of the government with respect to this process that there are restrictions or unfair limitations on the scope and function of the Auditor General. He himself drafted the proposed legislation. It was not presented directly to this House by the government; it was presented to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which as we know is headed by an opposition member.
The remarks made on television by the two members criticized the Auditor General for pitting his judgment, on matters of government policy, against that of the government. That is not his job and we should make that clear. We fully support the statements of our members in that respect. I fail to see how anyone can be critical of the proposed legislation. If anyone on the opposite side has any criticism of the way in which the Auditor General's act was drafted, I would like to hear it. I do not understand how there could be criticism because the Auditor General prepared the legislation, which is supposed to be restrictive in its scope. The truth of the matter is in the motion which reads as follows:
That this House condemns the government for criticizing the Auditor General of Canada for carrying out his duties according to law-
That is patently absurd.
-and reasserts its supports of the principle of unfettered parliamentary scrutiny of government expenditures-
There is no question about that.
-including the right of the Auditor General to comment on the failure of the government to make expenditure in strict compliance with parliamentary appropriation-
Criticism of Auditor General
There is no question about that. The following I think is the catchphrase:
-and to report on these and any other cases he feels should be brought to the attention of Parliament.
That is the area of this motion which I find unacceptable because it seems to delegate to the Auditor General the wide and sweeping right to criticize this Parliament in any way he wishes. It is not his function to criticize government policy, decisions, proposals, legislation and programs of every sort. That, Mr. Speaker, is an accurate and complete description of the role of the official opposition. In conclusion, I think we can very well understand why this motion has been put. The simple and plain reason why the opposition want the Auditor General to be able to carry out that function is because they now recognize their own dismal failure to do the job of the official opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is too much to hope that we would reach a point in some debate in this House at which a minister would be ready to admit, frankly and forthrightly, that he had said something which on sober, or drunken reflection-I do not care which-he had found to be wrong.
I would say in the presence of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), as I say it now in his absence, that his speech this afternoon was either a concoction deliberately designed to confuse everybody or else it was a rejection or retraction of the criticism he had made of the Auditor General in his broadcast.
