I hope it was the latter. Or it may have been both, as was suggested. I hope it was a retraction of that criticism. I would have respected the hon. gentleman a great deal more if he had possessed whatever was required-I am not going to find a word for
6134	COMMONS
Criticism of Auditor General it-to say frankly to this House and to the country that he had made a mistake. Then, at least, we would be discussing the issue of the Auditor General without all the exchanges which are now involved.
Backbenchers who participated in this debate would have given those of us who are in the opposition, and people who are outside, a great deal more confidence in their integrity and objectivity if they had said they would vote against the motion-I would not expect them to vote in favour of a motion of non-confidence against their own government-but that in their view the President of the Treasury Board had been wrong in what he said on television. It might be that those words came out of his mouth without sufficient thought having been given to them. I say this because of the kind of speech he made and the way in which this issue arose. It is disturbing, and it will continue to be disturbing as long as the hon. gentleman does not say in a forthright manner, "What I said on April 11 was wrong." So long as the President of the Treasury Board does not say this, we continue to be disturbed.
The issue arose out of what he said during that broadcast. Never mind the statement by the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) that it is necessary to put the minister's remarks in their context. Here is the context in itself. On April 11 he said that the Auditor General had "expressed his view as to the appropriateness of some government policies".
I ask hon. member to note the following words:
In this sense he is pitting his judgment as to sound business practice and sound government policy against the government's and, not unnaturally, you would not expect the government to agree with his judgment in every instance. I wonder, myself, whether the Auditor General should cast himself in this role, or whether we should look for, really, another kind of person to be Auditor General.
This is what gave rise to the fear in this House and in the country as to what the government intended to do with the position of Auditor General. If this is not what the President of the Treasury Board meant-and his speech today did not suggest this kind of thing-then he should have said so when he addressed the House. Many of us say things off the cuff in reply to questions on television and elsewhere which we might later regret. But in a matter of such importance as this, a minister, a member of the government-I see the hon. gentleman is now in the House, so I can use the word I did not use before-a minister should have the courage to say, "I

DEBATES	April 21, 1970
made a mistake in using the words I did; this is what I meant-" thereby removing the fear which is justifiable as long as those words remain on the record.
Two parts of the minister's statement are of particular importance. The first constitutes an objection to the Auditor General using his judgment as to what is sound business practice. Mr. Speaker, it is a basic duty of the Auditor General to analyse and, if necessary, to criticize the business practices of the government or any of its departments. For a minister to object to the Auditor General doing this is most disturbing. It is an illustration of the arrogance to which we have drawn attention so many times and it is part of the picture to which I shall refer later.
Then the President of the Treasury Board went on to say: "I wonder . .. whether we should look for, really, another kind of person to be Auditor General." If, in plain English, this does not mean that he-and presumably he speaks for the government-was contemplating kicking Mr. Henderson out of his job,
I	should like to know what those words do mean. This was a disturbing thing.
[DOT] (8:10 p.ra.)
Then today the President of the Treasury Board, both in his speech and I think in reply to some questions, said that this motion which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has moved is based on a wrong premise. At one point he said that it suggests there was criticism of the Auditor General. There is none, said the minister. Either he was telling the truth today or he was telling the truth on April 11. If he was telling the truth today, he should have said that what he said on April
II	was wrong. Then we would have had some kind of understanding of the basis on which this discussion is carried on. But so long as he leaves that statement on the record we have a right to be disturbed about the intentions of the government and of the President of the Treasury Board, despite the speech that he made this afternoon. If his speech was intended as a repudiation of what he said on April 11, I ask him to say so or to get somebody else to say so. If it is the case that he does repudiate it, then indeed he has the right to say that the motion is based on a wrong premise.
The fact is that much of the speech of the President of the Treasury Board today contained material with which all hon. members of the House agree. Many of the suggestions that he made for improving the relationship
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
between the Auditor General and the government would, I am sure, be accepted by the members of the Public Accounts Committee and most of the members of the House. I see nothing wrong in his suggestion that he or members of the government should be able to explain an action which is being criticized by the Auditor General. But the Auditor General has to retain his right to criticize. What did he say with regard to the concessions made to the automobile manufacturers? I should like to put on the record the sort of thing that he said.
What we on this side of the House are standing for, as I understood the Leader of the Opposition and my leader, what we are asking the government to accept is the right of the Auditor General to say these things. If there is an explanation to be given, then the minister should appear before the Public Accounts Committee to give it. He should satisfy the members of the Public Accounts Committee that what was done was the right thing; that the procedures that were followed were the right procedures; that the business practice that was employed was the right business practice.
If I may summarize what the Auditor General said, to save time, instead of reading his words, he said that the Tariff Order did not contain all of the criteria which the government applied in paying out over $180 million; that the fact was that one of the companies, the company that received $173 million, did not meet the criteria established in the Tariff Order, and that the government paid out money by Order in Council which, as I read the Auditor General, remitted or forgave payment and was not justified by the criteria in the only instrument which could justify it, namely, the Tariff Order. He said it is therefore essential that the Motor Vehicle Tariff Order, 1965, be amended to spell out all of the criteria to be followed in determining liability for payment of duty.
That, in summary, is what the Auditor General said and is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the Treasury Board objected to. It is because they objected to the Auditor General saying what it is his duty to say that we in the opposition believe the government ought to be castigated and that the members who have the courage to do so ought to vote for the motion and tell the government they must stop that sort of thing.
This is part of a picture that we have seen ever since this government took office. I cite
DEBATES	6135
Criticism of Auditor General the treatment by members of the government, particularly by the Prime Minister, of questions during question period and the attempt time and time again to make both Parliament and Members of Parliament look silly. Perhaps in some cases it may not be very hard to do that, including my own case. But that is not the job of the government. Let them leave it to us; we will do that on our own.
The general attitude toward Parliament by the government is characterized by an arrogance that apparently has no limit. Even the Auditor General is fair play for the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board whenever they feel like it. As pointed out by the two leaders who spoke this afternoon, the Auditor General is an essential part of the democratic process in this country, indeed in any democratic society.
It is important for Parliament and for the people of Canada to recognize that there are two kinds of policy matters. There is the policy matter that is concerned with the actual program that the government is given legislative authority to introduce and to implement. Then there is the policy that sets out the way in which the government's program and expenditures are in fact implemented.
The policy respecting the way in which expenditures are in fact implemented is precisely within the sphere of the Auditor General to study, to analyse and if necessary to criticize in order to improve the policy by which expenditures are carried through. The procedures that are used and whether or not there is legislative sanction for the way in which this is done are both part of the function of the Auditor General, as clearly described in section 67 and following sections of the Financial Administration Act.
With only 15 minutes in which to speak and with mine almost up, it is difficult to cover everything. But it is the readiness with which the President of the Treasury Board, more directly than the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), says that the Auditor General is stepping over the mark, and therefore that the government has to look for somebody else, that has disturbed the members of the opposition and is a condemnation of a government which wants to curtail the freedom and opportunity for work that the Auditor General in fact must have, and does have, under the legislation.
Finally, may I say that if the President of the Privy Council speaks this evening he will perhaps fill the gap which has been left. Even
April 21, 1970

Criticism of Auditor General in his speech this afternoon the President of the Treasury Board said that the Auditor General must not enter into policy matters. He said he must not lend himself to becoming part of the "adversary situation in Parliament", with which everyone agrees. But by saying that he is suggesting that the Auditor General has in fact lent himself to being part of the adversary situation in Parliament, and that is a pretty serious charge.
If I were the Auditor General, I would by implication consider that that was a pretty serious charge. I am not saying that the minister said that in so many words. Perhaps I would have respected it more had he done so. But by saying that the Auditor General must not permit himself to become part of the adversary game in Parliament, the President of the Treasury Board is implying that the Auditor General has in fact done so.
As I say, if I were Mr. Henderson I would consider that a pretty serious charge. I would say, as I say now to the President of the Treasury Board, that he had no right to make that statement unless he was willing to document the truth of it. This he did not do. Even in his speech this afternoon there was not a single word about the policies with which the Auditor General is supposed to have interfered. There was not a single word about the way in which he is supposed to have helped whatever it is that the President of the Treasury Board meant by the "adversary situation" in this Parliament. That is mere innuendo.

speechtext:
During his speech today there was more innuendo than in all the speeches made by the President of the Treasury Board. This motion is divided into two parts. The second part reads that this House-
-reasserts its support of the principle of unfettered parliamentary scrutiny of government expenditures including the right of the Auditor General to comment on the failure of the government to make expenditure in strict compliance with
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
parliamentary appropriations and to report on these and any other cases he feels should he brought to the attention of Parliament.
I think we all agree 100 per cent with that part of the motion. As the President of the Treasury Board said this afternoon, that is taken almost word for word from the statute itself, and as the law of Parliament we fully support it. I fully support it and would not suggest it should ever be changed in any way. However, the first part of the motion states:
That this House condemns the government for criticizing the Auditor General of Canada for carrying out his duties according to law-
I cannot and will not support that part because surely it is not true. This afternoon the President of the Treasury Board stated he had never made any such criticism and neither had the government. I saw the television program in question on which the statement of the President of the Treasury Board was supposed to have been made. This was one of those television programs on which a minister sits before a panel of journalists and is grilled by them over a period of time. It was one of those programs during which they deal with many subjects.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: The minister could defend himself better.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT

Maybe he could. That is another of those arrogant remarks the hon. member for York South interjects in speeches. I know very well that the President of the Treasury Board is capable of defending himself, but I feel that if this is a worthwhile motion I should give my point of view.
As I said, I watched that program. The questions put to the minister related to many subjects. For the most part they dealt with the situation in respect of the Post Office. The interviewers bombarded the minister with questions, and he handled himself in a very cool way: I thought he handled himself very well. When we come to the particular statement when he was talking about the Auditor General, he said-I do not have the exact words but the hon. member for York South had the transcript and read them into the record-something to the effect that we should look for another kind of person, or another person for this role.
I must admit that I had doubt as to what he meant. I did not know what the President of the Treasury Board meant when he said that. The questioner who heard his remark must also have had some doubt in his mind because within very few minutes he put a
DEBATES	6137
Criticism of Auditor General question directly to the President of the Treasury Board, asking if this meant that the government was trying to get rid of the Auditor General or to restrict his role. The President of the Treasury Board replied directly and categorically that they were not. I would think that if members of the opposition really had the courage to be honest, they would admit that this reply clarified the issue. The hon. member for York South was talking about courage this evening. As far as I am concerned, that reply settled the issue for me and I think it settled it for the people who were questioning the minister that day.
The next morning I saw a large headline in the Montreal Gazette to the effect that the President of the Treasury Board wanted to tamper in some way or another with the role of Auditor General. Of course, this is the type of headline we very often see in our papers: it is the result of a journalist looking for innuendoes and for division, for scandal or any type of weakness in words in order to make some kind of complaint against ministers or Members of Parliament whether they be on the government or the opposition side.
I saw that program, and the original doubt I had in my mind about the statement was completely cleared up by the very categorical statement made by the minister later in the program. On the following Monday and Tuesday questions were put not only to the President of the Treasury Board but to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). They were asked whether there was any intention on the part of the government to restrict the role of the Auditor General or to replace him. On every occasion they said no, and it was very clear that they said no.
This afternoon the President of the Treasury Board repeated this denial. Not only did he say the government did not want to tamper in any way with the role of the Auditor General, but he said it was the government's intention to make the role of the Auditor General more independent and to give him greater control over his office. He said it was the intention to take his salary out of the statute and tie it to that of a judge of the new federal court.
As a matter of fact, the recommendation this afternoon of the minister went much beyond the requests in the report of the Auditor General in which he asked for certain improvements in his office and in his role. I feel that this type of motion put before
April 21, 1970

Criticism of Auditor General us by the opposition is an attempt to create an issue. There are not enough real issues to deal with, so the opposition is trying to create one by putting forward a motion like this.
In his speech this afternoon the President of the Treasury Board said there were four general issues which emerged from the recent report of the Auditor General. The first relates to the independence of his office, the second to his role and responsibility, the third to the responsibility of the government to respond to the criticisms which he advances, and the fourth to the status of the Auditor General and his office. As I pointed out, the minister stated that all these recommendations had the support of the government and the government was willing to move on them and even go beyond those made by the Auditor General.
The minister also admitted that the government had perhaps not been as effective as it might have been in responding to some of the criticisms of the Auditor General. He stated the government was willing to take steps to improve this situation. He also stated he would recommend that the government be obliged to give a report each year in which it would answer to the House of Commons in respect of recommendations put forward by the Auditor General, and that this report would be considered by the Public Accounts Committee at the same time as the report of the Auditor General.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
In conclusion I wish to make very clear tha I fully support the role of the Auditor General and the present Auditor General in his job. I think we must protect him in that position and I believe he has every right to put forward his criticism in respect of waste, misappropriation and, as the minister stated this afternoon, probity. I do not think, however, that he should be in any way implicated in any type of policy discussion or pushed into any type of partisan role. Perhaps when the government brings forward its bill this matter will be clarified. The minister stated that on the whole the government would be dealing with the requests of the Auditor General himself in respect of this bill. I felt I should speak in the debate because there has been some doubt about this question and I wished to make clear my position on the matter and state that I intend to vote against both the amendment and the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my reason for speaking to

the motion is that I wish to leave no doubt in the mind of anyone within the sound of my voice this evening how I intend to vote. I intend to support the motion and I should like to give some of the reasons for my position. The previous speaker mentioned that he could not support the first part of the motion, which I believe is the part which should be supported. I belong to the school of people who believe that when members of a government make public utterances they are advancing the general policy of the government. So when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) make public utterances I believe it is appropriate that the public in general, in this case the people of Canada, should consider they speak for the government. On that basis the motion does condemn the government, but I submit the government deserves to be condemned for this particular reason.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The motion condemns the government criticizing the Auditor General of Canada for carrying out his duties according to law. Some members who have spoken this afternoon take exception to this language. Personally I do not take exception to it for the reasons I have just given the House. When two members of the government make public utterances concerning a dedicated public official and a man who occupies a position of great public trust, or when they make critical speeches concerning him, this becomes the policy of the government and deserves the condemnation of every member of this House.
I submit that this motion is also a motion of confidence in the Auditor General. I have the honour to sit on the Public Accounts Committee. It is a privilege to sit on that committee. I find that the attitude of the Auditor General toward public questions and toward the various inquiries which he makes by reason of his official position is an extremely fair one. I have never seen any indication of anything which I thought savoured of anything more than a reference to the actual facts which he could substantiate.
I have had some experience with auditors general in another capacity and I submit that in my opinion the government, or any government generally speaking should appreciate having an official of the importance of the Auditor General giving it honest-to-goodness
April 21, 1970	COMMONS
opinions concerning policy as well as facts. I have never been interested in hiring people in my business who were just yes, yes people. I prefer to have someone who will disagree with me and say, "Mr. Flemming, you are wrong about so and so and should change your mind about such and such". To me that is the proper type of person to be giving advice to a government, an individual or people interested in the public welfare. Therefore, I submit that it is not in the best interests of the country for any member of the government to advance the idea that the Auditor General must not under any condition or circumstance say anything which could be construed as being a reflection on public policies. It is important that the Auditor General should feel free to do this, and it is better for the government because the government should benefit from his advice.
I have spoken about the office of the Auditor rtpnpral and mv conception of what the Auditor General should do in his public capacity. Now for a moment I wish to refer to the general reputation the present incumbent of this office has in the hearts and minds of the Canadian people. He has been referred to as the guardian of the public purse. That is a good description. He has been referred to as the protector of the taxpayer. I say, with great respect, God knows that is needed. He has been referred to as the watchdog of the treasury. According to what we hear, this government needs a watchdog. But why would anyone hire a watchdog and then try to prevent it from barking? That, apparently, is what this government wants to do. I submit that all these descriptions indicate a _ great degree of confidence and public trust in the Auditor General. This motion not only condemns the government but expresses confidence in the Auditor General. This is another reason to vote for it. This confidence is well-deserved.
Generally speaking, all members who have spoken today on this subject have indicated their complete confidence in the Auditor General, but recent events lead us to believe the government does not share this opinion. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the previous speaker have referred to legislation that will be brought down in this House and we as members will be asked to consider and vote on it in the public interest. As the Prime Minister said the other day, this legislation will define the duties of the Auditor General. I submit the inference to be taken by the House is that the legislation will restrain the

Criticism of Auditor General Auditor General from fulfilling his functions to a certain degree, because when you define duties and go to the trouble of putting them down on paper it means you are not satisfied that the person holding the office is not overstepping the bounds of his authority.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Let us look at the Auditor General's authority. From where does he derive it? The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) gave the answer to that question this afternoon. My friend, the hon. member for Grey Simcoe (Mr. Noble) read from the document this afternoon. The hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Jerome) who spoke just before the supper break complained that the Auditor General had no business bringing these matters before Parliament and that he was exceeding his authority.
All the hon. member needs to do is examine page 1 of the Auditor General's report for 1968. Reference has been made to tnis passage today, but I will read it again. It says that the Auditor General shall call attention to every case in which he has observed certain situations, and then it goes on to say: and to any other case that the Auditor General considers should be brought to the notice of the House of Commons.
That is his statutory authority. I submit it is pretty broad authority, and I think properly so. The government should welcome it because it has the effect of giving advance notice to all, in connection with the spending of public funds, that an accounting will be demanded, that the record shall be kept very carefully, and that discrepancies of any nature will be included in the report of the Auditor General and brought before Parliament which, after all, consists of the representatvies of the people. That is as it should be.
Mr. Speaker, I support the motion, first because it condemns the government, which should be condemned, and second because it is an expression of confidence in the Auditor General. Those are two very good reasons for supporting the motion. There are other reasons.
I think that when notice is served on us that legislation will be changed, we have to be careful. Only a few days ago I had the privilege of speaking in this House on the hate literature bill. I said that legislation such as this had not been thought of for almost half a century, and I asked why we had it before us. I ask now, why do we have to
April 21, 1970

Criticism of Auditor General redefine the duties and responsibilities of the Auditor General, if it is not for the purpose of clipping his wings? In my opinion that is the reason for the government bringing in the legislation. They are most unwise in doing so. It will probably carry by virtue of the government's majority, but so far as I am concerned it is most unwise.
As I said, we have had some experience with auditors general. I have found them to be highly dedicated men: I have never found one who was otherwise. Certainly the present incumbent is no exception-quite the opposite. I think we must of necessity consider what has been stated by the President of the Treasury Board in connection with the Auditor General. Mr. Henderson has uncovered case after case of government waste, extravagance, and bureaucratic bungling which have cost the taxpayers millions of dollars.
It is obvious that his persistent criticism of the government's slipshod methods, mishandling of public funds, its irregular administrative practice are irritating and outraging the present cabinet. So when the President of the Treasury Board was questioned as to whether the Auditor General should cast himself in the role in which he pits his judgment against that of the government, he said, "Perhaps we should look for, really, another kind of person to be Auditor General".
I agree with the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) when he asked that the President of the Treasury Board clarify that statement. He should tell this House what he is looking for in an Auditor General. If he thinks we should have another kind of person, he should tell us what he is looking for. I submit that the Auditor General's function is to point out these irregularities to Parliament. I have no doubt that he is aware of what he is doing and I do not consider that he has made any attempt to pass judgment on government policies.
The House will remember that not very long ago various items of this nature were before the Public Accounts Committee. I think that the government chooses the wrong time-income tax time-to criticize the Auditor General. Canadians who will be paying their taxes within the next two weeks are bound to support the Auditor General who has shown where the government wasted $39J million last year. The taxpayer looking at a T-4 slip and wondering how he will pay his bills with the little bit of money left after the government gets through extracting money from the pay cheque-this applies pretty 
much to all of us-is bound to support the Auditor General. He will find it difficult to agree that the Auditor General should have his wings clipped. Mr. Henderson pointed out that the government had built an $8,800,000 port in the lower St. Lawrence region despite studies which showed there was no ship traffic there at all.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House is a very serious one and I regret the necessity for it. Even after all these years there seems to be some misconception in the highest quarters as to what the Auditor General's job is and what our duties are with regard to it. He has been castigated in absentia, which is a cowardly act, and if we do not defend him with this motion I do not know where he will be defended. The foolish part of it is that his action and service are of such an outstanding nature as to need no defence, and I am almost ashamed to find myself in the position of advocate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
As so often happens, Mr. Speaker, it becomes a matter of one side of the chamber calling down the other for its mistake, but of course I stand to be corrected. If the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) did not mean what he said, he did not dispel my doubts when he spoke this afternoon. If the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) did not mean what he said, he has yet to make any statement which would dispel my doubts.
As a public servant, the Auditor General has no opportunity to defend himself and I would be delinquent indeed if as a member of the Public Accounts Committee I did not do my best to defend him. His crime, according to the President of the Treasury Board, is that he has usurped the prerogative and power of the cabinet and has taken upon himself legislative authority. But, Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board was trying to do by the back door what he did not have the courage to do by the front door.
Referring to a series of recommendations concerning the office of the Auditor General made by the Public Accounts Committee in 1966-67, the Auditor General in 1969 reported as follows:
The committee is of the opinion that all of the characteristics, duties and functions of the office of the Auditor General should be set out in a separate act of Parliament governing this office instead of being a part of the Financial Administration Act.
The committee is requesting the Auditor General to consult his legal advisers and to co-operate with them in drafting such an act for submission to the committee and to the government.
If there is a crime-I use that word advisedly, Mr. Speaker-then it is ours. If the Auditor General has been remiss in his duties, as far as I can see it is only in carrying out the wishes of a committee which is the link between Parliament and his very important and efficient office. I think that argument disposes of any suggestion that he has exceeded his duties. Indeed, had he not carried out our wishes I would be quite prepared to move, in the Public Accounts Committee, that he be asked to explain why, after being given two years to work upon it, he had not come forward with a suitable act.
I might go further and say that perhaps our committee had been delinquent in not taking more immediate action on this matter, had it not been for the fact that it is powerless to act until given the opportunity to meet under the authority of this House. We have often complained that we do not sit long enough or often enough to go into detail on very important matters.
Another misdemeanour of which the Auditor General was accused is the language used in his report. I do not know what kind of language he was supposed to use to explain, in dollars and cents, the negligent spending of our money. He is obliged to outline non-productive expenditures, but these have been interpreted as having some deep, dark meaning.
In 1961 the Public Accounts Committee, chaired by one of the most beloved members of the House, the previous Speaker and now a member of the other place, put forward the suggestion that each and every year the Auditor General should "list in the minutest detail all non-productive items which come to his attention."
If the Auditor General has erred, in my opinion and in the opinion of many within the sound of my voice he has only erred in performing his duties too well. He has in fact listed in his report, to the best of his knowledge and to the best of the ability of his staff, all the non-productive items coming to his attention. We could split hairs by arguing whether the adjectives used were correct, whether the spending of this money was negligent, criminally negligent or extravagant. I do not think the adjectives mean anything at the recommendation stage. If our feelings are that tender it might be suggested that the report be kept secret until the Public Accounts Committee, the body to which this report belongs, has approved it and that until then it should remain a privileged document.
April 21, 1970

Criticism of Auditor General
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The Auditor General's duty, as I see it, is plain. He must act entirely in an advisory capacity to our committee. No matter what his opinions might be, so long as they are honest we, representing a cross section of the Canadian people, will look at them as carefully as we can and in as detailed a manner as possible in the time at our disposal. Only after we have made our recommendations is the government obliged to take any further steps. It can take steps without our advice, as it has on many occasions, and it can ignore our advice, as it has on a great many occasions.
Since our recommendations have been ignored over and over again during the past years, it is not surprising that our chief adviser-I am talking about the adviser to the Public Accounts Committee-should become a little impatient. The Auditor General would be a poor adviser indeed if he did not point out these leaks in the treasury.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: And the extravagances.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
They appear to be extravagances, certainly; they run into tens of millions, and in some cases hundreds of millions of dollars. We are not just dreaming in this regard. I am impressed by the very restrained language which our Auditor General uses. He does not use inflammatory language; he uses language showing that he is alarmed as a good accountant, as perhaps the best accountant in Canada who has the confidence of the Canadian people and of the United Nations. He runs his office so efficiently that accounting departments of the great universities in Canada today recognize training in the Auditor General's department as being equivalent to apprenticeship in any firm of auditors of which the universities have cognizance.
It is not strange that the Auditor General, whose job is to discover horses on the payroll, the sale of railways between senior members of the armed forces and other matters that ought to come to the public's attention, should use adjectives which are not complimentary. It would be passing strange if he always used weak and subdued language in a great, dynamic young democracy like Canada. The people would not compliment the Auditor General nor our committee if this type of sloppiness and criminal negligence-those adjectives are of my choosing-were allowed to run unchecked.
I am shocked that any member of the government, let alone a cabinet member, should pour his venom on a man who is not in a

position to defend himself. Something even more sinister may be behind this. The Auditor General was relatively secure so long as he did not tread on the really big, sacred cows. Unless I am mistaken, his criticism of the automotive pact really brought onto his head the fire from high places.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to express my view on the motion before the House and, particularly, on the work being done by our Auditor General, Mr. Henderson. I am a member of the Public Accounts Committee. During the previous year and this year I took a great deal of interest in the Auditor General's report and in the material which he brought to the attention of the Public Accounts Committee for investigation.
It seems to me that the recent attack launched against the Auditor General by two prominent ministers is extremely regrettable. It does something, I believe, to this institution and to the position of the Auditor General which all the words in the world cannot undo. It is regrettable particularly that those in the seats of power should see fit to criticize someone who, in my humble opinion, is doing the very job this House has told him to do. He is doing it ably and I believe he is doing it honestly. Of course, other members have said this.
The Auditor General is the watchdog over government spending and I believe it is absolutely essential that this House should in no way restrict his freedom to investigate, analyse and report his findings on every aspect of government spending. Any move by the present government to restrict a full and thorough review of spending by federal government departments will be a negation of democracy.
We boast about the rights of the citizens of Canada to full information on all and every government expenditure. I am certain that Canadians would not tolerate any move by the federal government or any government which would prevent this type of financial information being made public. The criticism in public of the Auditor General by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) in my opinion is a disgraceful and unwarranted attack on an individual who is carrying out the duties assigned to him by this House.
April 21, 1970

In part VII of the Financial Administration Act, Revised Statutes, chapter 116, it very clearly indicates that everything the Auditor General has done to date has been within the confines of the regulations laid down by this House of Commons. I am not going to go over them all again, but the act lists them and at the very bottom it adds that the Auditor General is entitled to look into any other things that he considers should be brought to the attention of the House of Commons. This is all the Auditor General and his assistants need to look into government expenditures and find out where foolish and faulty expenditures have been made. These are included in his report and it is then up to the committee to find out why these expenditures were made and what has been done year after year by the departments to correct stupid governmental spending. I think the Auditor General's Department is being handled in the way it should.
Any hon. member of this House who tries to put a muzzle on an individual who is pointing out fields of foolish public expenditure does not deserve to sit in this House, because this is the very essence of democracy. We are here as elected members from every part of Canada. We are spending the taxpayers' money. Not only do we spend the taxpayers' money as elected Members of Parliament but we are here to make sure we get good value for every dollar spent. What do we find? We find two responsible cabinet members on television and over the air telling the people of Canada that this is not the type of searchlight we want on the expenditures of this nation.

thorough job they should be doing. Every time a discrepancy is found by the Auditor General, the taxpayers of Canada save money. If we as Members of Parliament were doing the job we should be doing, we would make absolutely certain there was not a repetition of the stupid spending of public money which year after year we find in some departments of government. I am not saying that the departmental heads are dishonest. I am not saying that at all. However, many of these departments are so wide-flung that the man in charge loses control over the expenditures.
It is the job of the Auditor General to delve and find out where the errors are being made and to bring this to the attention of the House. It is up to us to do the rest. What would happen if we took the advice of the government and had the Auditor General doing strictly the job of accounting, making certain that the money is not being misappropriated in any way? If that were the case, hardly anyone in this House would have the slightest knowledge of what was going on behind the scenes.
It is the job of the Auditor General and his staff to dig in and find out where department heads and far-flung department areas are getting into financial trouble, and report back to us. Some of the cabinet members still have the audacity to stand and say that this man must be removed because he is embarrassing the government.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we know that for some months the government has been after the Auditor General's head. First the government was suspicious when he noticed the extravagant and scandalous expenditures for the building of the Bonaventure. The government's ire was stirred and today it wants to table a bill for the purpose of redefining the auditor general's role. It is a way of forcing him to tender his resignation, which would please the government greatly, because then he could be replaced by an obliging and docile character who would follow the dictates of the President of the Treasury Board and the President of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Order, please. It being 9.45 o'clock p.m. it is my duty, pursuant to section 9 of Standing Order 58, to interrupt these proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the motion now before-the House.
The question is on the amendment. All those in favour of the amendment will please say yea.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Yea.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: All those opposed will please-say nay.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Nay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
In my opinion the nays have-it.
And more than five members having risen:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Call in the members.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
But we in the opposition do not agree with this view of the government.
Moreover, it would appear that there is no unanimity within the cabinet. The President of the Treasury Board said on television that the Auditor General had to be replaced. However the President of the Privy Council declared that a bill must be introduced to redefine the responsibilities of the Auditor General.
The other day, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) seemed to be taking side with the Auditor General when he said that there was no difference between the views of the Auditor General and those of the government.
Mr. Speaker, as long as the government does not acknowledge the relevance of the Auditor General's duties, the role of this important official in the administration of the country will simply be reduced to nothing because this government, since it came to power, has seemed to want to govern without taking into account the views of hon. members or those of the nation. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, we shall fight valiantly so that the Auditor General might keep his responsibilities, that Parliament might, with him, discuss and study thoroughly the expenditures which the government would like to hide from the people.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-CRITICISM OF AUDITOR GENERAL BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. The question is now on the main motion. All those in favour of the main motion will please say yea.
